title: The Shrewd Manager and the Rich Man and Lazarus
summary: Jesus tells of a manager who, about to be fired, reduces his master's debtors' bills to win friends, and draws lessons about using money faithfully and the impossibility of serving both God and money. When the money-loving Pharisees scoff, he answers them about the Law and divorce, then tells the story of a rich man who ignored a beggar named Lazarus at his gate and found the roles reversed after death.
story: Luke's long account of Jesus' travel toward Jerusalem continues. Chapter 15 ended with three parables of lost things found, told to Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that Jesus ate with sinners. Now Jesus turns to his disciples, with the Pharisees still listening, and speaks about money, a subject Luke returns to more than any other Gospel writer. The chapter is framed by two parables that both begin with a rich man. The first shows a man using wealth with an eye on his future; the second shows a man who used it with no eye on anything beyond his own table. Between them stands a warning that the kingdom now being preached does not cancel the Law but fulfills it.
historical:
Large estates in first-century Galilee and Judea were often owned by wealthy landlords, some living elsewhere, and run by managers (stewards) who handled rents, loans, and contracts on their behalf. Tenants frequently paid in produce, which explains debts measured in olive oil and wheat. A hundred measures of oil and a hundred measures of wheat were substantial amounts, well beyond a peasant's household needs, so these debtors were likely tenant farmers or merchants. Interpreters differ on what the manager actually did. Some think he simply cut his master's income dishonestly; others suggest he removed his own commission, or a hidden interest charge that the Law of Moses forbade Israelites to take from one another (Deuteronomy 23:19-20). Either way, the master is caught: the debtors now praise his generosity, and he cannot easily reverse it.

The saying on divorce (verse 18) enters a live debate. Deuteronomy 24:1 permitted a man to divorce his wife if he found some indecency in her, and rabbinic tradition remembers the schools of Shammai and Hillel disagreeing over how broadly that phrase should be read, the stricter view limiting it to sexual wrongdoing and the looser allowing divorce for lesser causes. In that world only the husband could initiate divorce under Jewish law. Jesus' saying, stricter than either school, protected wives from being discarded at will.
cultural:
Jesus calls money mammon (verses 9, 11, and 13), an Aramaic word for wealth or property. By setting it beside God as a rival master, he treats it almost as a power that claims service. The comment that the Pharisees were lovers of money reflects a common assumption in the culture that wealth was a sign of God's approval, an assumption the story of the rich man overturns. Purple cloth, dyed with an expensive extract from sea snails, was a mark of royalty and great wealth; fine linen, much of it imported from Egypt, was costly clothing.

Lazarus lies at the rich man's gate, meaning the gate of a large house with a courtyard. Dogs in that world were scavengers, not pets, and their licking his sores makes his helplessness and uncleanness vivid. Abraham's side (literally his bosom) pictures the place of honor next to the host at a banquet, where a guest reclined against the one beside him. Hades was the Greek name for the realm of the dead, and the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made in the centuries before Jesus) used it for the Hebrew Sheol. Jewish writings of the period described the dead as held in separate places awaiting judgment, and stories of rich and poor exchanging fortunes after death circulated in the ancient world. Jesus uses that familiar picture to make a point about listening to Moses and the prophets.
literary: The chapter pairs two parables, both opening with the words there was a rich man, around a short set of sayings (verses 14 to 18) that respond to the Pharisees' scoffing. The first parable ends with the master's surprising praise, then a chain of sayings loosely linked by key words: faithful, unjust, wealth, true riches, master. The second parable falls into two scenes, life (verses 19 to 21) and death (verses 22 to 31), with a reversal between them: the man who had everything now begs for a drop of water from the man who had nothing. Apart from Abraham, Lazarus is the only character in any of Jesus' parables who is given a personal name. Its meaning, God has helped, fits the story. The rich man is never named. The parable ends not with a verdict but with a warning that points forward: “they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.”

outline.t: The parable of the shrewd manager
Faithfulness with money; God or money
The Pharisees scoff; the Law, the kingdom, and divorce
The rich man and Lazarus in life
The reversal after death and the great chasm
The request for the brothers: Moses and the prophets

doctrines.note: Jesus says, “You cannot serve both God and money.” Wealth becomes a rival master when it commands the loyalty that belongs to God. The chapter treats the love of money not as a minor weakness but as a competing worship.

The story of the rich man and Lazarus assumes that death is not the end, that life's choices carry consequences beyond it, and that there comes a point where the chasm is fixed. It teaches that the time to heed God's word is now.

Abraham's answer, “They have Moses and the prophets; let your brothers listen to them”, affirms that Scripture is sufficient to call people to repentance. Even a miracle will not persuade those who refuse the word already given.

words.note: Mammonas, wealth. The word comes from Aramaic and means money or possessions. The BSB renders it worldly wealth and money. Jesus personifies it as a master competing for service, which is why older translations kept the word Mammon.

Oikonomos, manager or steward: literally one who manages a household. The word later becomes a picture of Christian responsibility, as Paul calls apostles stewards of the mysteries of God. The parable's point rests here: what we hold is not ours but our master's, and we will give account for it.

Hades, the realm of the dead. In Greek usage it named the underworld; in the Septuagint it translates Sheol, the shadowy place of the dead. Here it is a place of torment separated from Abraham's side. The New Testament more often uses Gehenna for final judgment, and interpreters debate whether Hades here refers to the intermediate state between death and resurrection or to final punishment.

christ: The chapter's last line carries a shadow of what is coming. Abraham says that those who will not listen to Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. Luke's readers knew that someone did rise, and that many still did not believe. In chapter 24 the risen Jesus himself points his disciples back to Moses and all the prophets to explain his death and resurrection. The chapter also shows Jesus' authority over the Law: he does not loosen it (not a stroke of a pen will drop out) but presses it deeper, into marriage and money. And his concern for the poor man at the gate reflects the mission he announced in Nazareth, good news to the poor (4:18).

hard.q: Why would Jesus praise a dishonest manager, and is the story of Lazarus a literal picture of the afterlife?
hard.a:
In the first parable it is the master, not Jesus, who commends the manager, and he commends him for acting shrewdly, not for his dishonesty. Jesus draws a comparison from the lesser to the greater, as he does with the unjust judge in chapter 18: if worldly people plan so cleverly for their earthly future, how much more should the children of light use money with eternity in view. Some interpreters soften the manager's guilt by suggesting he removed his own commission or an illegal interest charge; others think the point works precisely because he was a rogue.

On the second parable, readers differ. Some take it as a real account of the state of the dead, since it names a person and gives details. Most interpreters read it as a parable that uses a familiar Jewish picture of the afterlife to teach about wealth, repentance, and Scripture, without meaning to map the geography of the unseen world. Both readings agree on what the story clearly teaches: that the choices of this life matter beyond it, that God sees the poor, and that there is a point after which it is too late.

questions: Jesus says whoever is faithful with very little will be faithful with much. What small, everyday uses of money or time reveal what you actually serve?
The rich man never harmed Lazarus; he simply did not see him. Who lies at your gate that is easy not to see?
Abraham says those who ignore Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded by a resurrection. What does that suggest about the relationship between evidence and willingness to believe?
